title: Time series change points
text: mcp implements AR MA generalized ARMA (GARMA) recurrence response-family link scale. \eta^{\text{reg}}_t ordinary linear predictor segment formulas \eta_t linear predictor including serial dependence, \begin{aligned} \text{AR}_t &= \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_{j,t} \left[g(y^*_{t-j}) - \eta^{\text{reg}}_{t-j}\right] \\ \text{MA}_t &= \sum_{k=1}^{q} \theta_{k,t} \left[g(y^*_{t-k}) - \eta_{t-k}\right] \\ \eta_t &= \eta^{\text{reg}}_t + \text{AR}_t + \text{MA}_t \end{aligned} \phi_{j,t} lag-j autoregressive (AR) coefficient time t, \theta_{k,t} lag-k moving-average (MA) coefficient time t, g(\cdot) link function (g(\mu_t) = \eta_t, \mu_t = g^{-1}(\eta_t)), y^*_t threshold-constrained observation threshold constant c (set via threshold = 0.1 default). Thus ar() uses lagged link-scale residuals relative ordinary regression, ma() uses lagged one-step innovations. mcp regression change points coefficients \phi_{j,t} \theta_{k,t}. See applied examples. Unavailable lags beginning series contribute zero. recurrence used JAGS, fitted values, predictions, log likelihoods, fresh-series simulation. key feature recurrence AR/MA memory flows continuously across change points: order-N component new segment, last N observations change point input first \eta_t new segment, weighted new segment’s AR/MA parameters. AR/MA lags reset segments; memory flows continuously one segment next. Lags reset beginning dataset, independent series using series = "column_name" (see Multiple time series). change point locations \tau estimated posterior uncertainty, change point AR/MA parameters switch varies conditionally across MCMC draws. GARMA currently supports default links gaussian() (identity), binomial() (logit), bernoulli() (logit), poisson() (log), negbinomial() (log). Non-default links rejected now. Warning: AR MA coefficients modeled directly jointly constrained stationary invertible regions. higher-order terms ar(2), independently bounded coefficients can violate usual root conditions. Coefficients change across predictors segments, ar(1, 1 + x) model = list(y ~ ar(1), ~ ar(1)), instead define time-varying process usual constant-coefficient conditions directly apply. applies ma().

what: Priors on AR and MA coefficients
title: Time series change points
text: Brief overview default priors default prior AR MA intercept truncated normal distribution: symmetric around zero gently shrinks away [-1, 1] bounds: central 95% interval approximately [-0.84, 0.84]. regularizing prior direct coefficient, joint stationarity invertibility constraint orders one. brms also models AR MA coefficients directly within [-1, 1], uses flat default priors range. Thus mcp keeps familiar parameter interpretation adding mild regularization toward zero; fits generally similar likelihood informative. Categorical contrasts default dnorm(0, 0.25). Slopes also normal scaled predictor’s SD, dnorm(0, 0.25 / sd(column)). Thus approximately 95% prior change per SD predictor lies within \pm 0.5. defaults express assumption sign. time series positive first-order autocorrelation expected, alternatives include ar1_1 = "dunif(0, 1)" ar1_1 = "dnorm(0.5, 0.5) T(0, 1)". Read specifying checking priors. complete list (default) priors model : can also visualize priors sampled prior. prior = TRUE works mcp functions, including plot() summary().  Notice density estimates smoothed sharp cutoffs, T(-1, 1) bounds, slightly misrepresenting true distribution. Let’s inspect priors advanced AR model, since often inform : AR MA coefficient regressions use identity link, residual inputs use supported response-family link described . Careful priors become especially important higher orders coefficient slopes, individual values [-1, 1] ensure stable recurrence. fitting, mcp() checks 500 posterior draws 100 observed predictor rows warns checked-draw violation rate exceeds corresponding ar ma threshold diagnostics (10% default). fit$simulate() checks supplied coefficient trajectory generating fresh series. predictor- segment-varying coefficients local smoke tests, proofs global stationarity invertibility. ways may want inform AR MA parameters: constant AR(2) process, stationarity requires -1 < \phi_2 < 1 \phi_2 - 1 < \phi_1 < 1 - \phi_2. One dependent-prior construction stays region ar2_1 = "dunif(-1, 1)" together ar1_1 = "dunif(ar2_1 - 1, 1 - ar2_1)". simpler suggestion ar2_1 = "dunif(0, ar1_1)" sufficient. Higher orders require corresponding joint root condition. Slopes can quickly make AR coefficients non-stationary MA coefficients non-invertible. Set prior scale relative plausible change observed range x. example, shallow negative change observed range use "dnorm(0, 0.1 / (max(x) - min(x))) T(, 0)".

code: fit$jags_code ## model { ##   # Change points ##   cp_0 = min(year) ##   cp_1 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_3)  # Flat Dirichlet on the segment lengths ##   cp_2 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_3)  # Flat Dirichlet on the segment lengths ##   cp_3 = max(year) ##   cp_order_ ~ dbern(step(cp_2 - cp_1))  # Ordered change points ##  ##   # Priors for population-level effects ##   Intercept_1 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(1.5)^2)   # Link-scale intercept, approximately uniform on the probability scale ##   year_2_end_ ~ dnorm(Intercept_1, 1/(0.043121968093205169*(cp_2-cp_1))^2)   # Autoscaled link-scale coefficient (rstanarm autoscaling); sampled as the value at the segment end ##   year_2 = (year_2_end_ - (Intercept_1)) / (cp_2 - cp_1) ##   Intercept_3_end_ ~ dnorm(year_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2), 1/(1.5)^2)   # Link-scale intercept, approximately uniform on the probability scale; sampled as the value at the segment end ##   Intercept_3 = Intercept_3_end_ - (year_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2)) ##   year_3 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(0.043121968093205169)^2)   # Autoscaled link-scale coefficient (rstanarm autoscaling) ##  ##   # Model and likelihood ##   for (i_ in 1:length(year)) { ##     # year measured from each segment's change point ##     x_local_1_[i_] = min(year[i_], cp_1) ##     x_local_2_[i_] = min(year[i_], cp_2) - cp_1 ##     x_local_3_[i_] = min(year[i_], cp_3) - cp_2 ##      ##     # Formula for mu ##     link_mu_[i_] = ##       (year[i_] >= cp_0) * (year[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 +  ##       (year[i_] >= cp_1) * (year[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(year_2)) * x_local_2_[i_] +  ##       (year[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(Intercept_3)) * 1 +  ##       (year[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(4)], c(year_3)) * x_local_3_[i_] ##  ##     # Likelihood for family = binomial() ##     mu_[i_] = ilogit(link_mu_[i_]) ##     y[i_] ~ dbin(mu_[i_], N[i_]) ##   } ## }

sampled as the value at the segment end ##   x_3 = (x_3_end_ - (Intercept_2)) / (cp_3 - cp_2) ##   sigma_Intercept_1_mid_ ~ dt(-sigma_x_1 * 1 + sigma_x_1 * (25.875), 1/(2.5)^2, 3)   # Weakly regularizing modeled log-SD intercept; on the value at min(x); sampled as the value at the expected midpoint of segment 1 ##   sigma_Intercept_1 = sigma_Intercept_1_mid_ - (sigma_x_1 * (25.875)) ##   sigma_x_1 ~ dt(0, 1/(0.043193421279068007)^2, 3)   # Regularizing log-SD coefficient scaled by the predictor SD ##   sigma_Intercept_2 ~ dt(0, 1/(2.5)^2, 3)   # Weakly regularizing modeled log-SD intercept ##   sigma_x_3_end_ ~ dt(sigma_Intercept_2, 1/(0.043193421279068007*(cp_3-cp_2))^2, 3)   # Regularizing log-SD coefficient scaled by the predictor SD; sampled as the value at the segment end ##   sigma_x_3 = (sigma_x_3_end_ - (sigma_Intercept_2)) / (cp_3 - cp_2) ##   sigma_xE2_3_rise_ ~ dt(0, 1/(0.0002100945749551876*(cp_3-cp_2)^2)^2, 3)   # Regularizing log-SD coefficient scaled by the predictor SD; sampled as the rise over the segment ##   sigma_xE2_3 = sigma_xE2_3_rise_ / (cp_3 - cp_2)^2 ##  ##   # Model and likelihood ##   for (i_ in 1:length(x)) { ##     # x measured from each segment's change point ##     x_local_1_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_1) ##     x_local_2_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_2) - cp_1 ##     x_local_3_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_3) - cp_2 ##     x_local_4_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_4) - cp_3 ##      ##     # Formula for mu ##     link_mu_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * (x[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(Intercept_2)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(x_3)) * x_local_3_[i_] +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_3) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(4)], c(x_3)) * x_local_4_[i_] ##      ##     # Formula for sigma ##     link_sigma_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * (x[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(5)], c(sigma_Intercept_1)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * (x[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(6)], c(sigma_x_1)) * x_local_1_[i_] +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(7)], c(sigma_Intercept_2)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(8)], c(sigma_x_3)) * x_local_3_[i_] +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(9)], c(sigma_xE2_3)) * x_local_3_[i_]^2 ##  ##     # Likelihood for family = gaussian() ##     mu_[i_] = link_mu_[i_] ##     sigma_[i_] = max(1e-05, exp(link_sigma_[i_])) ##     y[i_] ~ dnorm(mu_[i_], 1 / sigma_[i_]^2) ##   } ## }

Later segments use response, one-sided, ~ predictor, starts change point can modeled using cp(), e.g., ~ cp((1 | id)) + 0 + x. cp() change-point part formula rest predictor part, works like lm()/glm()/brms::brm(). 1. Response (segment 1 ): y ~ ...: Standard continuous, binary, count response (Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, negative binomial). successes | trials(total) ~ ...: Binomial response (family = binomial()). y | weights(w) ~ ...: Observation log-likelihood weights (multiplies observation’s log-likelihood contribution w > 0; affects posterior inference log_lik(), predictions). y | trials(total) + weights(w) ~ ...: Combine response auxiliaries using +. 2. Change-point part (cp(), segments 2+): ~ x (.e., cp() included): Population-level change point (default). ~ cp(1) + x. ~ cp((1 | id)) + x: Group-level change-point deviations around population-level change point (read ). intercept implicit, cp(1 + (1 | id)). 3. Predictor part (segments): ~ 1 + x: Disjoined slope new segment intercept. ~ 0 + x: Joined slope (new intercept). ~ 1: Plateau (intercept , slope). ~ x:state + z + (1 | id): variables, interactions, group-level effects (read ). + sigma(1 + x) shape(0 + state): Distributional parameters link scale. code: fit$jags_code ## model { ##   # Change points ##   cp_0 = min(x) ##   cp_1 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_2)  # Uniform within the observed range of x ##   cp_1_id_sd ~ dnorm(0, 1/(24.716320808511227)^2) T(0,)  # Group-level change-point SD before truncation ##   for (id_ in 1:n_unique_id) { ##     cp_1_id_location[id_] ~ dnorm(cp_1, 1/(cp_1_id_sd)^2) T(cp_0, cp_2)  # Group-level change-point deviations, truncated between the neighboring change points ##     cp_1_id[id_] = cp_1_id_location[id_] - cp_1  # deviation from population change point ##   } ##   cp_2 = max(x) ##  ##   # Priors for population-level effects ##   Intercept_1 ~ dnorm(25.186470821654748, 1/(18.620544312604412)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default) ##   x_2 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(0.64588420009064662)^2)   # Autoscaled mean coefficient (rstanarm default) ##   sigma_1 ~ dt(0, 1/(5.3)^2, 3) T(0,)  # Positive residual SD calibrated on the response scale ##  ##   # Model and likelihood ##   for (i_ in 1:length(x)) { ##     # x measured from each segment's change point ##     x_local_1_[i_] = min(x[i_], (cp_1_id_location[id_index_[i_]])) ##     x_local_2_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_2) - (cp_1_id_location[id_index_[i_]]) ##      ##     # Formula for mu ##     link_mu_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= (cp_1_id_location[id_index_[i_]])) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(x_2)) * x_local_2_[i_] ##      ##     # Formula for sigma ##     link_sigma_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(sigma_1)) * 1 ##  ##     # Likelihood for family = gaussian() ##     mu_[i_] = link_mu_[i_] ##     sigma_[i_] = max(1e-05, link_sigma_[i_]) ##     y[i_] ~ dnorm(mu_[i_], 1 / sigma_[i_]^2) ##   } ## }

code: # Model parameters x = 1:20 cp_1 = 12 Intercept_1 = 5 Intercept_2 = 10  # Ifelse version y_ifelse = ifelse(x <= cp_1, yes = Intercept_1, no = Intercept_2)  # Indicator equivalent using dummy helpers cp_0 = -Inf cp_2 = Inf y_indicator = (x > cp_0) * (x <= cp_1) * Intercept_1 +  # Between cp_0 and cp_1               (x > cp_1) * (x <= cp_2) * Intercept_2  # Between cp_1 and cp_2  # Show it par(mfrow = c(1,2)) plot(x, y_ifelse, main = "ifelse(x <= cp_1)") plot(x, y_indicator, main = "(x > cp_1) * Intercept_2") library(mcp) model = list(y ~ 1, ~ 1) fit = mcp(model, data = data.frame(y = 1:10, x = 1:10), sample = FALSE, par_x = "x") fit$jags_code ## model { ##   # Change points ##   cp_0 = min(x) ##   cp_1 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_2)  # Uniform within the observed range of x ##   cp_2 = max(x) ##  ##   # Priors for population-level effects ##   Intercept_1 ~ dnorm(5.5, 1/(7.5691258852437295)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default) ##   Intercept_2 ~ dnorm(5.5, 1/(7.5691258852437295)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default) ##   sigma_1 ~ dt(0, 1/(3.7)^2, 3) T(0,)  # Positive residual SD calibrated on the response scale ##  ##   # Model and likelihood ##   for (i_ in 1:length(x)) { ##     # x measured from each segment's change point ##     x_local_1_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_1) ##     x_local_2_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_2) - cp_1 ##      ##     # Formula for mu ##     link_mu_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * (x[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(Intercept_2)) * 1 ##      ##     # Formula for sigma ##     link_sigma_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(sigma_1)) * 1 ##  ##     # Likelihood for family = gaussian() ##     mu_[i_] = link_mu_[i_] ##     sigma_[i_] = max(1e-05, link_sigma_[i_]) ##     y[i_] ~ dnorm(mu_[i_], 1 / sigma_[i_]^2) ##   } ## }

what: How mcp implements slope changes in JAGS using indicators
title: From formulas to sampler code
text: Bayesian MCMC samplers like JAGS evaluate dynamic conditional statements (/else) parameters sampled. implement piecewise model JAGS, mcp uses indicator plateauing formulation (evaluated via Iverson brackets [] equal 1 true 0 false). First, mcp defines span X_{k,} measures x change point within segment k stays constant beyond : X_{1,} = \min(x_i, \tau_1) X_{k,} = \max\bigl(0, \min(x_i, \tau_k) - \tau_{k-1}\bigr) \quad (k \ge 2) x_i < \tau_{k-1}, X_{k,} = 0 (segment). \tau_{k-1} \le x_i < \tau_k, X_{k,} = x_i - \tau_{k-1} (linear growth within segment). x_i \ge \tau_k, X_{k,} = \tau_k - \tau_{k-1} (constant segment width). purely joined model (list(y ~ 0 + x, ~ 0 + x)), mcp writes \eta_i cumulative sum segment spans: \eta_i = \sum_{k=1}^K [x_i \ge \tau_{k-1}] \cdot \beta_{k,1} X_{k,} segment’s contribution stays constant beyond change point (\beta_{k-1,1}(\tau_{k-1} - \tau_{k-2})), joining needs restrictions parameters: earlier segments provide starting value later segments. expected response response scale \mu_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i) via link function g(\mu_i) = \eta_i (identity Gaussian, \mu_i = \eta_i). segment disjoined (~ 1 + x), introduces new intercept \beta_{k,0} \tau_{k-1}, earlier terms get indicator [x_i < \tau_{k-1}] end disjoined segment starts. Terms x-terms get indicator next change point, end . Let’s demonstrate equivalence R:  Let us see action: used options(mcp_reparam = FALSE) see plain model. default, mcp samples parameters scales, return . Look JAGS code # x measured segment's change point # Formula mu see exact indicator formulation action: x_local_1_[i_] x_local_2_[i_] correspond X_{1,} X_{2,}, segment’s slope multiplied indicator (e.g., (x[i_] >= cp_1)). fitted(), predict(), log_lik(), etc. evaluate exact formula R. See model R.
code: # Model parameters x = 1:20 cp_1 = 12 slope_1 = 2 slope_2 = -1  # Ifelse version y_ifelse = ifelse(x <= cp_1,              yes = slope_1 * x,             no = cp_1 * slope_1 + slope_2 * (x - cp_1))  # Indicator version with local plateauing coordinates (pmin is vectorized min) y_local = slope_1 * pmin(x, cp_1) +            (x > cp_1) * slope_2 * (x - cp_1)  # Show that both formulations are identical par(mfrow = c(1,2)) plot(x, y_ifelse, main = "ifelse() version") plot(x, y_local, main = "Local plateauing coordinate") model = list(y ~ 0 + x, ~ 0 + x) old = options(mcp_reparam = FALSE)  # Write the plain model fit = mcp(model, data = data.frame(y = 1:10, x = 1:10), sample = FALSE) options(old) fit$jags_code ## model { ##   # Change points ##   cp_0 = min(x) ##   cp_1 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_2)  # Uniform within the observed range of x ##   cp_2 = max(x) ##  ##   # Priors for population-level effects ##   x_1 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(2.5)^2)   # Autoscaled mean coefficient (rstanarm default) ##   x_2 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(2.5)^2)   # Autoscaled mean coefficient (rstanarm default) ##   sigma_1 ~ dt(0, 1/(3.7)^2, 3) T(0,)  # Positive residual SD calibrated on the response scale ##  ##   # Model and likelihood ##   for (i_ in 1:length(x)) { ##     # x measured from each segment's change point ##     x_local_1_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_1) ##     x_local_2_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_2) - cp_1 ##      ##     # Formula for mu ##     link_mu_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(x_1)) * x_local_1_[i_] +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(x_2)) * x_local_2_[i_] ##      ##     # Formula for sigma ##     link_sigma_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(sigma_1)) * 1 ##  ##     # Likelihood for family = gaussian() ##     mu_[i_] = link_mu_[i_] ##     sigma_[i_] = max(1e-05, link_sigma_[i_]) ##     y[i_] ~ dnorm(mu_[i_], 1 / sigma_[i_]^2) ##   } ## }

text: dirichlet(alpha) \alpha > 1 default prior multiplied weight \prod_k s_k^{\alpha - 1}, s_k relative segment lengths (see math). JAGS lets specify priors built-distributions, multiply prior arbitrary factor directly. standard workaround “zeros trick”: add observed data point whose likelihood equals factor. mcp passes cp_weight_ = 0 data models cp_weight_ ~ dpois(lambda). probability observing 0 Poisson distribution e^{-\lambda}, \lambda = -(\alpha - 1) \sum_k \log s_k, likelihood exactly weight. Since s_k \le 1, \lambda \ge 0 \alpha \ge 1, dpois() requires. also \alpha < 1 supported. example, dirichlet(2) two change points adds line: cp_order_, cp_weight_ observed data (0), weights cp_* parameters likelihood. title: Poisson and negative-binomial change point analysis
text: dataset coal mining disasters grown popular change point literature (available boot::coal). contains timestamp coal mining disaster 1851 1962. counting number events within year (fixed time frame), something Poisson-friendly. Note years without disasters must included zeros: number events (n) function year (date) typically modeled change two intercepts. simple mcp: Let us see two intercepts (lambda log-units) change point (years): can see model ran well good convergence large effective sample sizes. first glance, change point estimated lie years 1886 1897 (95% interval). Let us take direct look, using default mcp plot:  seems fit data well, can see change point probability “lumps” around particular data points. Years low number disasters abruptly increase probability change lower disaster rate taken place. posterior distributions change points regularly take “weird” forms, .e., well-described toolbox parameterized distributions. can see clearly plotting posteriors. include traceplot , just check convergence visually.
code: # Number of disasters by year, including years with zero disasters (no data rows) year = factor(floor(boot::coal$date), levels = 1851:1962) df = data.frame(date = 1851:1962, n = as.vector(table(year)))  # See it head(df) ##   date n ## 1 1851 4 ## 2 1852 5 ## 3 1853 4 ## 4 1854 1 ## 5 1855 0 ## 6 1856 4 library(mcp) future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3) model = list(   n ~ 1,  # intercept-only   ~ 1  # intercept-only )  fit = mcp(model, data = df, family = poisson(), par_x = "date") result = summary(fit) result ## Family: poisson ## Links: mu = log ## Draws: 9000 (3 chains with iter = 3000) ## Segments: ##   1: n ~ 1 ##   2: ~ 1 ##  ## Change point parameters: ##    parameter     mean    sd    lower    upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail ##  cp_1        1890.5   2.5   1886.1   1896.5   1.00     1944      990 ##  ## Population-level parameters: ##    parameter     mean    sd    lower    upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail ##  Intercept_1    1.131 0.094    0.944    1.313 1.00     4302     4741 ##  Intercept_2   -0.09  0.13    -0.35     0.15  1.00     4472     5006 plot(fit) plot_pars(fit)

title: Poisson and negative-binomial change point analysis
text: Brief overview default priors poisson() defaults link = 'log', meaning exponentiate estimates get “raw” Poisson parameter \lambda. \lambda nice property mean number events. rate around 3.1 disasters per year segment 1 0.91 segment 2. Exponentiating posterior mean log-rate gives approximately posterior median \lambda, mean. posterior mean, exponentiate draws averaging, e.g., mean(exp(as_draws_df(fit)$Intercept_1)), use fitted(fit). intercept prior normal distribution centered rounded median log(n), zeros replaced 0.1 (brms), scale equal maximum 2.5 rounded MAD. Replacing zeros keeps log finite minimum scale avoids accidentally narrow prior. Coefficients autoscaled rstanarm, e.g., dnorm(0, 2.5 / sd(column)), group-level SDs default half-normal priors. normal priors avoid infinite expected counts heavier Student-t tails imply log link (read ). default prior change point restricts observed range. coefficient priors deliberately broad defaults, update informed priors particular case possible, e.g.:
code: prior_summary(fit) ## # A tibble: 3 × 5 ##   parameter   segment dpar  prior             bounds                ##   <chr>         <int> <chr> <chr>             <chr>                 ## 1 cp_1              2 NA    dunif(1851, 1962) [1851, 1962], ordered ## 2 Intercept_1       1 mu    dnorm(0, 2.5)     none                  ## 3 Intercept_2       2 mu    dnorm(0, 2.5)     none prior = list(   cp_1 = "dnorm(1900, 30) T(min(date), 1925)" ) fit_with_prior = mcp(model, data = df, family = poisson(), prior = prior, par_x = "date")

Harmonizing log-mean coefficients, intercept contrasts default dnorm(0, 2.5) slopes dnorm(0, 2.5 / sd(column)) (group SDs default dnorm(0, ...) T(0, )). brms uses flat coefficients Student-t intercept, mcp uses proper normal priors avoid heavy tails pull shape toward extreme overdispersion. Shape regression can weakly identified, informed priors may useful.

title: Poisson and negative-binomial change point analysis
text: modeling event counts exposure (e.g., person-years, area, population size) varies across observations, can model rates \lambda = \text{Count} / \text{exposure} log link supplying offset(log(exposure)): fitted() returns expected counts given row’s exposure. get expected rates per unit exposure, set exposure 1 newdata, offset \log(1) = 0: works way predict(), returns predicted counts unit exposure. fitted(..., rate = TRUE) argument apply Poisson negative-binomial models; binomial models, converts counts proportions trials. Adding categorical predictor model, can also model rate ratios. offset present, mcp automatically shifts default intercept prior centering observed log-counts observed log-rates (\log(y) - \text{offset}), keeping minimum scale 2.5. Note par_x vs. cumulative exposure: offset evaluated per row local exposure observation. par_x represents continuous cumulative time origin (e.g., [0, t_i]), using offset(log(par_x)) integrate piecewise rates across prior segments; instead, current segment’s rate applied total duration. data consists discrete time intervals (bins) duration \Delta t_i, using offset(log(delta_t)) valid.
code: # Example: Event counts over varying observation durations (as here) or population model = list(   events ~ 1 + year + offset(log(exposure)),  # Segment 1   ~ 1 + year + offset(log(exposure))          # Segment 2 )  fit = mcp(model, data = df, family = poisson())  # implicit link = "log" fitted(fit, newdata = transform(df, exposure = 1))

title: Poisson and negative-binomial change point analysis
text: Despite popularity dataset, question rarely asked evidence change point . Let us fit two models without change points use approximate leave-one-cross-validation see predictive performance two models compare. flat model one-decay model. intercept mcp date = 0, far data, measure decay first year ((date - 1851)) reduce posterior correlation intercept slope. helps sampling:  Now compute compare LOO ELPDs: flat model clearly worse, elpd_diff / se_diff around 4, disaster rate decrease. change point model preferred decay model, difference smaller standard error. diag_elpd column also flags observations high Pareto k values change point model, PSIS-LOO estimate less reliable. Taken together, data clearly distinguish abrupt change gradual decay. Another approach look model weights: , change point model preferred weights show ranking implied loo_compare, decay model retains non-negligible weight.
code: # Fit an intercept-only model fit_flat = mcp(list(n ~ 1), data = df, family=poisson(), par_x = "date") fit_decay = mcp(list(n ~ 1 + I(date - 1851)), data = df, family = poisson(), par_x = "date")   plot(fit_flat) + plot(fit_decay) fit_loo = loo(fit) ## Warning: Some Pareto k diagnostic values are too high. See help('pareto-k-diagnostic') for details. fit_flat_loo = loo(fit_flat) fit_decay_loo = loo(fit_decay) loo::loo_compare(fit_loo, fit_flat_loo, fit_decay_loo) ##   model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse       diag_diff      diag_elpd ##  model1       0.0     0.0      NA                 4 k_psis > 0.7 ##  model3      -3.2     3.6    0.82 |elpd_diff| < 4                ##  model2     -32.9     8.3    1.00 ##  ## Diagnostic flags present. ## See ?`loo-glossary` (sections `diag_diff` and `diag_elpd`) ## or https://mc-stan.org/loo/reference/loo-glossary.html. loo_list = list(fit_loo, fit_flat_loo, fit_decay_loo) loo::loo_model_weights(loo_list, method="pseudobma") ## Method: pseudo-BMA+ with Bayesian bootstrap ## ------ ##        weight ## model1 0.794  ## model2 0.000  ## model3 0.206

what: JAGS code for the Poisson example
title: Poisson and negative-binomial change point analysis
text: JAGS code full Poisson change-point model .
code: fit$jags_code ## model { ##   # Change points ##   cp_0 = min(date) ##   cp_1 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_2)  # Uniform within the observed range of date ##   cp_2 = max(date) ##  ##   # Priors for population-level effects ##   Intercept_1 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(2.5)^2)   # Robustly centered log-count intercept with a minimum scale of 2.5 ##   Intercept_2 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(2.5)^2)   # Robustly centered log-count intercept with a minimum scale of 2.5 ##  ##   # Model and likelihood ##   for (i_ in 1:length(date)) { ##     # date measured from each segment's change point ##     x_local_1_[i_] = min(date[i_], cp_1) ##     x_local_2_[i_] = min(date[i_], cp_2) - cp_1 ##      ##     # Formula for mu ##     link_mu_[i_] = ##       (date[i_] >= cp_0) * (date[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 +  ##       (date[i_] >= cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(Intercept_2)) * 1 ##  ##     # Likelihood for family = poisson() ##     mu_[i_] = exp(link_mu_[i_]) ##     n[i_] ~ dpois(mu_[i_]) ##   } ## }

title: Working with priors
text: mcp takes priors form named list. names parameter names, values distribution strings, constants, names parameters. fairly complicated example, demonstrate various ways priors can used: Distribution strings use JAGS names argument order, including T() truncation, JAGS distributions generally allowed (see JAGS user manual). However, JAGS code: mcp uses conventional scales instead JAGS precision, .e., SD dnorm(), SD log scale dlnorm() (sdlog stats::dlnorm()), scale dt(), ddexp(), dlogis(). generating JAGS code, mcp converts inverse variance dnorm(), dt(), dlnorm(), inverse scale ddexp() dlogis(). can inspect translation comparing fit$prior fit$jags_code. notes: Change points always ordered (cp_1 < cp_2 < ...), whatever priors. See priors change points. mcp allows inserting data-dependent terms: example, min(x), max(x), mean(y), median(y), sd(y), mad(y), max(x) - min(x), n_segments(), n_cp(). mcp resolves expressions generating JAGS code. older mcp v0.3.4 uppercase constants (MINX, MAXX, ) remain temporarily supported deprecation warning. can fix parameter specific value. Simply set numerical value (cp_2 ). constant 100% prior belief value, therefore estimated. reuse coefficient later segment, prefer () model, e.g., ~ 1 + (x) segment 3. reuses x_2 instead estimating x_3. Equating parameters prior (x_3 = "x_2" ) gives fit keeps x_3 duplicate. Read () Understanding mcp formulas. can write deterministic expressions x_3 = "x_2 + 5 - cp_1/10". Since x_3 now deterministic given x_2 cp_1, leaves one fewer free parameter estimate. Let us see priors running mcp compare default priors: Now, let’s simulate data model. following priors “odds” actual data show effect. Sample prior posterior. First, let’s look priors side side. Notice use prior = TRUE show prior draws. works plot(), plot_pars(), summary() among others.  resulting posterior fits:  see effects priors: intercept Intercept_1 truncated 10. slope x_1 restricted bounds dbeta(), .e., 0 1. slopes x_2 x_3 forced identical. change point cp_2 constant, uncertainty . cp_1 still ordered , .e., prior dnorm(30, 10) restricted min(x) < cp_1 < 80. title: Working with priors
text: JAGS code fit_manual. See formulas sampler code implements priors change points.
code: fit_manual$jags_code ## model { ##   # Change points ##   cp_0 = min(x) ##   cp_1 ~ dnorm(30, 1/(10)^2) T(cp_0,cp_3)  # User-specified prior, truncated to the observed range of x, restricted to ordered change points ##   cp_2 = 80  # Fixed at 80 ##   cp_3 = max(x) ##   cp_order_ ~ dbern(step(cp_2 - cp_1))  # Ordered change points ##  ##   # Priors for population-level effects ##   Intercept_1 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(5)^2) T(,10)  # User-specified prior ##   x_1 ~ dbeta(2, 5)  # User-specified prior ##   Intercept_2_end_ ~ dnorm(24.321850954171083 + x_2 * (cp_2 - cp_1), 1/(26.856367009148308)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default); sampled as the value at the segment end ##   Intercept_2 = Intercept_2_end_ - (x_2 * (cp_2 - cp_1)) ##   x_2 ~ dt(0, 1/(1)^2, 3) T(x_1,)  # User-specified prior ##   Intercept_3_end_ ~ dnorm(24.321850954171083 + x_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2), 1/(26.856367009148308)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default); sampled as the value at the segment end ##   Intercept_3 = Intercept_3_end_ - (x_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2)) ##   x_3 = x_2  # Same value as x_2 ##   sigma_1 ~ dt(0, 1/(9.9)^2, 3) T(0,)  # Positive residual SD calibrated on the response scale ##  ##   # Model and likelihood ##   for (i_ in 1:length(x)) { ##     # x measured from each segment's change point ##     x_local_1_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_1) ##     x_local_2_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_2) - cp_1 ##     x_local_3_[i_] = min(x[i_], cp_3) - cp_2 ##      ##     # Formula for mu ##     link_mu_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * (x[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * (x[i_] < cp_1) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(x_1)) * x_local_1_[i_] +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_1) * (x[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(Intercept_2)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_1) * (x[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(4)], c(x_2)) * x_local_2_[i_] +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(5)], c(Intercept_3)) * 1 +  ##       (x[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(6)], c(x_3)) * x_local_3_[i_] ##      ##     # Formula for sigma ##     link_sigma_[i_] = ##       (x[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(7)], c(sigma_1)) * 1 ##  ##     # Likelihood for family = gaussian() ##     mu_[i_] = link_mu_[i_] ##     sigma_[i_] = max(1e-05, link_sigma_[i_]) ##     y[i_] ~ dnorm(mu_[i_], 1 / sigma_[i_]^2) ##   } ## }

title: Regression with Multiple Change Points
text: articles mcp website go -depth functionality mcp. executive summary, give quick sense mcp can . Understanding mcp formulas: Parameter names Intercept_i (intercepts), cp_i (change points), x_i (slopes), ar*/ma* (autocorrelation), sigma_* (Gaussian residual standard deviation). terms included segment get coefficients . ~ 0 + ... joined: continues earlier intercept x-terms (x, state:x, (x^2)) left . ~ 1 + ... disjoined starts afresh. Use (z) reuse coefficient preceding segment. change point model basically ifelse model ordered change points. Generate data supported models using fit$simulate(). See examples , e.g., mcp_example("demo")$example_code. Supported families link functions: mcp currently supports specific combinations families (gaussian(), binomial(), bernoulli(), poisson(), negbinomial()) link functions (identity, logit, probit, log). using informative priors incorporate expert knowledge. Use binomial(link = "logit") binomial change points mcp. Also relevant bernoulli(link = "logit"). Use negbinomial(link = "log") poisson(link = "log"). Read Poisson negative binomial change points mcp. Get results linear-predictor (link) scale rather response scale using plot(fit, scale = "linear") fitted(fit, scale = "linear"). Model comparison hypothesis testing: Leave-One-Cross-Validation using loo(fit) loo::loo_compare(loo1, loo2). Compute Savage-Dickey density ratios using hypothesis(fit, "cp_1 = 40"). Group-level (random) effects: Model group-level intercepts, slopes, change points using (1|id), (0 + x||id), cp((1|id)). Get posteriors using ranef(fit) deviations coef(fit) group-specific values. Plot using plot(fit, facet_by = "my_group") plot_pars(fit, pars = "group", type = "dens_overlay", ncol = 3). Group-specific change points restricted observed range x ordered within group. Modeling autoregression distributional parameters like Gaussian residual standard deviation: ~ 0 + sigma(1) models intercept change standard deviation. ~ 0 + sigma(0 + x) models increasing/decreasing standard deviation. Explicit sigma() formulas use log link, coefficients log-SD scale. ~ ar(N) models Nth order autoregression residuals. ~ar(N, 0 + x) models increasing/decreasing autocorrelation. y | weights(w) (y | trials(N) + weights(w)) specifies observation log-likelihood weights (w > 0) across families. can provide complete models distributional parameters (currently sigma(), shape(), mu()) time-series (ar() ma()). example, ~ x + sigma(1 + x:state) models abrupt change followed -state slopes variance. Get fitted predicted values intervals: fitted(fit) predict(fit) take many arguments predict -sample --sample values intervals. Forecasting prior knowledge future change points. Plotting: plot(fit, interval = c("fitted", "predict")) shows fit central intervals. Use color_by, facet_by, models several predictors. plot_dpar(), plot_pars(), pp_check() plot distributional parameters, parameters, posterior predictive checks. return ggplot2 objects, interpolate_newdata() helps make plots. Using priors: See priors fit$prior prior_summary(fit) set priors using mcp(..., prior = list(cp_1 = "dnorm(0, 1)", cp_2 = "dunif(0, 45)")). Default priors weakly informative, conventional defaults rstanarm intercepts coefficients brms scale parameters, documented deviations. default prior change points flat Dirichlet prior segment lengths (read ). Fix parameters specific values using cp_1 = 45. reuse coefficient later segment, use () model, e.g., ~ 0 + (x). Truncate priors using T(lower, upper), e.g., Intercept_1 = "dnorm(0, 1) T(0, )". Change points always ordered. Set minimum segment length using, e.g., cp_2 = "dunif(cp_1 + 20, max(x))". prior predictive checks using mcp(model, data, sample = "prior") |> plot(prior = TRUE). Missing responses posterior imputation: Missing responses imputed jointly parameters. Use fitted(fit) |> filter(.na(y)) expected responses predict(fit) |> filter(.na(y)) posterior imputations. plotting missing responses, asking probabilistic questions , etc. Tips, tricks, debugging Speed fitting using future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3), /fewer iterations, mcp(..., warmup = 500). text: x mcpfit object. ... Must empty. Reserved future use. hypotheses String representation logical test involving model parameters. Takes R code evaluates TRUE FALSE vectorized way. Directional hypotheses specified using <, >, <=, >=. hypothesis returns posterior probability \(P(H \mid \text{data})\) Bayes factor favor stated hypothesis \(H\): $$\text{BF}_{10} = \frac{P(H \mid \text{data}) / (1 - P(H \mid \text{data}))}{P(H) / (1 - P(H))}$$ \(P(H)\) prior probability \(H\). Bayes factor requires prior posterior draws mcp(sample = ""). example: "cp_1 > 30":  first change point 30. "Intercept_1 > Intercept_2": intercept greater segment 1 2. "x_2 - x_1 <= 3": difference slope 1 2 less equal 3. "Intercept_1 > -2 & Intercept_1 < 2": Intercept_1 -2 2 (interval hypothesis). can useful Region Practical Equivalence test (ROPE). "cp_1^2 < 30 | (log(x_1) + log(x_2)) > 5": creative. "`cp_1_id[John]` > `cp_1_id[Mary]`": John's change point later Mary's, estimated group-level change-point deviation id change point 1 (starting segment 2). Note `` required around names [level]. Equality hypotheses use equal sign (=) Savage-Dickey density ratio: posterior density divided prior density tested point equality \(\theta = \theta_0\): $$\text{BF}_{01} = \frac{p(\theta = \theta_0 \mid \text{data})}{p(\theta = \theta_0)}$$ \(\theta\) evaluated parameter (affine contrast), \(\theta_0\) hypothesized null value, \(p(\theta = \theta_0 \mid \text{data})\) posterior density, \(p(\theta = \theta_0)\) prior density. Bayes factor nested point-null model fitted continuous model (\(\text{BF}_{10} = 1 / \text{BF}_{01}\)). Prior posterior draws required, using mcp(sample = ""). point-null model's nuisance prior fitted model's conditional prior equality. Equality tests limited named scalar parameters affine contrasts. Examples: "cp_1 = 30": compare point-null model cp_1 = 30 continuous alternative. text: mcp model divides change-point variable \(x\) \(K\) segments separated ordered change points \(\tau_1 < \dots < \tau_{K-1}\). segment \(k \\{1, \dots, K\}\), linear predictor \(\eta_i\) measures \(x\) change point \(\tau_{k-1}\): $$\eta_i = \alpha_k + \beta_{k,1} (x_i - \tau_{k-1}) \quad (\text{} \tau_0 = 0)$$ \(\alpha_k\) value start segment \(k\): $$\alpha_k = \begin{cases}   \beta_{k,0}, & \text{disjoined } (\sim \texttt{1 + x}, \text{ } k = 1) \\   \alpha_{k-1} + \beta_{k-1,1} (\tau_{k-1} - \tau_{k-2}), & \text{joined } (\sim \texttt{0 + x}) \end{cases}$$ , disjoined segment starts intercept \(\beta_{k,0}\), joined segment continues segment \(k-1\) left . , \(\beta_{k,1}\) slope \(x\) segment \(k\). Intercepts slopes absolute values (changes relative preceding segments). variables (e.g., + z + state) add \(\sum_j \gamma_{k,j} z_{j,}\) segments included. use original values part \(\alpha_k\), can make joined segment start jump. inverse-linked parameter \(\mu_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i)\) via link function \(g(\mu_i) = \eta_i\), representing expected response families (success probability binomial models, expected count \(n_i \mu_i\)). Distributional parameters (sigma(), shape(), etc.) autoregressive terms (ar(), ma()) follow exact segmented structure respective link scales. Since segmented linear predictor, mcp calls distributional parameters (dpar): mu, sigma, shape, AR/MA lag (ar1, ar2, ma1, ...), e.g., fitted(fit, dpar = "ar1") fixef(fit, dpar = "sigma"). text: Autoregressive (ar(p)) moving-average (ma(q)) terms define finite conditional recurrence link scale (generalized autoregressive moving-average, GARMA). support Gaussian (identity), binomial (logit), Bernoulli (logit), Poisson (log), negative-binomial (log) families. \(\eta^{\text{reg}}_t\) ordinary linear predictor segment formulas \(\eta_t\) linear predictor including serial dependence, recurrence decomposes components: $$\begin{aligned}   \text{AR}_t &= \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_{j,t} \left[g(y^*_{t-j}) - \eta^{\text{reg}}_{t-j}\right] \\   \text{MA}_t &= \sum_{k=1}^{q} \theta_{k,t} \left[g(y^*_{t-k}) - \eta_{t-k}\right] \\   \eta_t &= \eta^{\text{reg}}_t + \text{AR}_t + \text{MA}_t \end{aligned}$$ \(\phi_{j,t}\) lag-\(j\) autoregressive (AR) coefficient time \(t\), \(\theta_{k,t}\) lag-\(k\) moving-average (MA) coefficient time \(t\), \(g(\cdot)\) link function, \(y^*_t\) observation, constrained threshold constant \(c\) (argument threshold = 0.1 ar() / ma()) keep residuals finite link scale, e.g., \(y^*_t = \max(y_t, c)\) zero counts Poisson models. Available elements rhat = 1.01, ess_bulk = 400, ess_tail = 400, ar = 0.10, ma = 0.10. empty list uses defaults; partial list overrides supplied values. Set element NULL disable diagnostic, use FALSE disable configurable diagnostic warnings. summary.mcpfit(), NULL inherits settings used fit model, list FALSE overrides diagnostic footer. quiet Logical. Suppress routine JAGS output mcp sampling-status messages? Defaults FALSE. Use options(mcp_quiet = TRUE) change default session. cores Deprecated ignored. Configure parallel processing future plan instead, example future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3). default future plan, chains sampled sequentially. argument remains available backwards compatibility. adapt Deprecated; use warmup instead.

code: # \donttest{ # Define the segments using formulas. A change point is estimated between each formula. model = list(   response ~ 1,  # Plateau in the first segment (Intercept_1)   ~ 0 + time,    # Joined slope (time_2) in segment 2 which starts at cp_1   ~ 1 + time     # Disjoined slope (Intercept_3, time_3) at cp_2 )  # Fit it and sample the prior too. # future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3)  # Uncomment for parallel sampling data = mcp_example_data("demo")  # Simulated data example demo_fit = mcp(model, data = data, sample = "both", seed = 42)  # See parameter estimates summary(demo_fit) #> Family: gaussian #> Links: mu = identity; sigma = identity #> Draws: 9000 (3 chains with iter = 3000) #> Segments: #>   1: response ~ 1 #>   2: ~ 0 + time #>   3: ~ 1 + time #>  #> Change point parameters: #>    parameter   mean    sd  lower  upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail    sim match #>  cp_1        31.8   1.7   28.5   35.1   1.00     3249     4358 30.0      OK #>  cp_2        71.1   1.0   69.5   72.8   1.00     3660     6245 70.0      OK #>  #> Population-level parameters: #>    parameter   mean    sd  lower  upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail    sim match #>  Intercept_1  9.96  0.65   8.69  11.25  1.00     4919     6791 10.00     OK #>  time_2       0.547 0.048  0.456  0.643 1.00     5176     6667  0.500    OK #>  Intercept_3 13.9   1.4   11.3   16.7   1.00     2254     4267 15.0      OK #>  time_3      -0.205 0.084 -0.372 -0.039 1.00     1238     2159 -0.300    OK #>  sigma_1      3.87  0.29   3.35   4.47  1.00     5025     5407  3.50     OK  # Visual inspection of the results plot(demo_fit)  # Visualization of model fit/predictions  plot_pars(demo_fit)  # Parameter distributions   pp_check(demo_fit)  # Prior/Posterior predictive checks   # Test a hypothesis hypothesis(demo_fit, "cp_1 > 30") #> # A tibble: 1 × 7 #>   hypothesis     mean    sd lower upper  prob    BF #>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> #> 1 cp_1 - 30 > 0  1.75  1.74 -1.52  5.08 0.836  5.13  # Make predictions head(fitted(demo_fit)) #> # A tibble: 6 × 6 #>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper #>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> #> 1    12.2   76.3  12.9 1.01   10.9    14.9 #> 2     6.35  83.5  11.4 0.714  10.0    12.8 #> 3    28.0   60.2  25.5 0.897  23.7    27.2 #> 4    15.7   74.7  13.2 1.11   11.1    15.4 #> 5    16.2   85.9  10.9 0.708   9.54   12.3 #> 6    22.3   40.1  14.5 0.649  13.1    15.6 head(predict(demo_fit)) #> # A tibble: 6 × 6 #>   response  time .mean   .sd .lower .upper #>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> #> 1    12.2   76.3  12.9  3.97   5.01   20.8 #> 2     6.35  83.5  11.4  3.94   3.67   19.2 #> 3    28.0   60.2  25.4  3.96  17.6    33.3 #> 4    15.7   74.7  13.3  3.97   5.29   21.1 #> 5    16.2   85.9  10.9  3.96   3.18   18.7 #> 6    22.3   40.1  14.5  4.01   6.73   22.2 head(predict(demo_fit, newdata = data.frame(time = c(55.545, 80, 132)))) #> # A tibble: 3 × 5 #>    time .mean   .sd .lower .upper #>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> #> 1  55.5 23.0   3.94  15.2    30.7 #> 2  80   12.2   3.98   4.35   19.9 #> 3 132    1.44  5.59  -9.52   12.4  # Compare to a one-intercept-only model (no change points) with default prior model_null = list(response ~ 1) fit_null = mcp(model_null, data = data, par_x = "time")  # fit another model here demo_loo = loo(demo_fit) null_loo = loo(fit_null) loo_compare(demo_loo, null_loo) #>   model elpd_diff se_diff p_worse diag_diff diag_elpd #>  model1       0.0     0.0      NA                     #>  model2     -58.1     9.1    1.00                      # Inspect the prior. Useful for prior predictive checks. summary(demo_fit, prior = TRUE) #> Family: gaussian #> Links: mu = identity; sigma = identity #> Draws: 9000 (3 chains with iter = 3000) #> Segments: #>   1: response ~ 1 #>   2: ~ 0 + time #>   3: ~ 1 + time #>  #> Change point parameters: #>    parameter  mean    sd  lower upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail   sim match #>  cp_1        34    23      2    84    1.00     3984     5301 30       OK #>  cp_2        67    23     17    98    1.00     3496     5260 70       OK #>  #> Population-level parameters: #>    parameter  mean    sd  lower upper rhat ess_bulk ess_tail   sim match #>  Intercept_1 14    18    -20    48    1.00     9356     8910 10       OK #>  time_2      -0.01  0.63  -1.24  1.22 1.00     9087     8988  0.50    OK #>  Intercept_3 14    17    -21    48    1.00     8841     8553 15       OK #>  time_3       0.02  0.62  -1.22  1.23 1.00     9023     8947 -0.30    OK #>  sigma_1      6.3   7.3    0.2  25.0  1.00     8599     8635  3.5     OK plot(demo_fit, prior = TRUE)   # Show all priors. Default priors are added where you don't provide any prior_summary(demo_fit) #> # A tibble: 7 × 5 #>   parameter   segment dpar  prior                  bounds                     #>   <chr>         <int> <chr> <chr>                  <chr>                      #> 1 cp_1              2 NA    dunif(0.61863, 99.741) [0.61863, 99.741], ordered #> 2 cp_2              3 NA    dunif(0.61863, 99.741) [0.61863, 99.741], ordered #> 3 Intercept_1       1 mu    dnorm(13.825, 17.383)  none                       #> 4 time_2            2 mu    dnorm(0, 0.62124)      none                       #> 5 Intercept_3       3 mu    dnorm(13.825, 17.383)  none                       #> 6 time_3            3 mu    dnorm(0, 0.62124)      none                       #> 7 sigma_1           1 sigma dt(0, 5.7, 3) T(0, )   [0, Inf]                    # Set priors and re-run prior = list(   Intercept_1 = 15,   time_2 = "dt(0, 2, 1) T(0, )",  # t-dist slope. Truncated to positive.   cp_2 = "dunif(min(time), 80)"   # change point to segment 3 before 80 (and after cp_1). )  fit3 = mcp(model, data = data, prior = prior, seed = 42)  # Reuse coefficients in later segments using same() (e.g., Intercept_1 in segment 3) model_same = list(   response ~ 1,   ~ 0 + time,   ~ same(1, as = 1) + time  # Reuse Intercept_1 instead of estimating Intercept_3 ) fit_same = mcp(model_same, data = data, sample = FALSE)  # Show the JAGS model demo_fit$jags_code #> model { #>   # Change points #>   cp_0 = min(time) #>   cp_1 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_3)  # Flat Dirichlet on the segment lengths #>   cp_2 ~ dunif(cp_0, cp_3)  # Flat Dirichlet on the segment lengths #>   cp_3 = max(time) #>   cp_order_ ~ dbern(step(cp_2 - cp_1))  # Ordered change points #>  #>   # Priors for population-level effects #>   Intercept_1 ~ dnorm(13.825120048974153, 1/(17.382500430759464)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default) #>   time_2_end_ ~ dnorm(Intercept_1, 1/(0.62123709509255609*(cp_2-cp_1))^2)   # Autoscaled mean coefficient (rstanarm default); sampled as the value at the segment end #>   time_2 = (time_2_end_ - (Intercept_1)) / (cp_2 - cp_1) #>   Intercept_3_end_ ~ dnorm(13.825120048974153 + time_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2), 1/(17.382500430759464)^2)   # Mean intercept (rstanarm default); sampled as the value at the segment end #>   Intercept_3 = Intercept_3_end_ - (time_3 * (cp_3 - cp_2)) #>   time_3 ~ dnorm(0, 1/(0.62123709509255609)^2)   # Autoscaled mean coefficient (rstanarm default) #>   sigma_1 ~ dt(0, 1/(5.7)^2, 3) T(0,)  # Positive residual SD calibrated on the response scale #>  #>   # Model and likelihood #>   for (i_ in 1:length(time)) { #>     # time measured from each segment's change point #>     x_local_1_[i_] = min(time[i_], cp_1) #>     x_local_2_[i_] = min(time[i_], cp_2) - cp_1 #>     x_local_3_[i_] = min(time[i_], cp_3) - cp_2 #>      #>     # Formula for mu #>     link_mu_[i_] = #>       (time[i_] >= cp_0) * (time[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(1)], c(Intercept_1)) * 1 +  #>       (time[i_] >= cp_1) * (time[i_] < cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(2)], c(time_2)) * x_local_2_[i_] +  #>       (time[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(3)], c(Intercept_3)) * 1 +  #>       (time[i_] >= cp_2) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(4)], c(time_3)) * x_local_3_[i_] #>      #>     # Formula for sigma #>     link_sigma_[i_] = #>       (time[i_] >= cp_0) * inprod(rhs_matrix_[i_, c(5)], c(sigma_1)) * 1 #>  #>     # Likelihood for family = gaussian() #>     mu_[i_] = link_mu_[i_] #>     sigma_[i_] = max(1e-05, link_sigma_[i_]) #>     response[i_] ~ dnorm(mu_[i_], 1 / sigma_[i_]^2) #>   } #> } # }

text: name Name example. One : "ar": One change point autoregressive residuals (ar1 dpar) "binomial": Binomial two change points. Much like "demo" logit scale. "demo": Two change points intercepts joined/disjoined slopes. "group_mu": Group-level predictor deviations (random intercepts/slopes) across change point. "group_cp": Group-level change-point deviations (random effects). "intercepts": intercept-change point. "missing": Missing data imputation (NAs response variable y). "multiple": Multiple regression categorical predictors interactions. "sigma": change "sigma" dpar, including slope sigma. "void": Missing data around change points. sample One "post": Sample posterior. "prior": Sample prior. Use prior = TRUE explicitly plots, summaries, methods select prior draws. "": Sample prior posterior. Plots, summaries, etc. default using posterior. Use prior = TRUE select prior draws. "none" FALSE: sample. Returns mcpfit object without draws ("empty fit"). useful want check prior strings (fit$prior), JAGS model (fit$jags_code), etc. plot Logical. Plot fitted example? Requires sample != "none".

code: # \donttest{ fit = mcp_example("multiple")  print(fit$example_code) # See how the data was simulated #> # Define model #> model = list( #>   y ~ 1 + x:state + z, #>   ~ 1 + x + state, #>   ~ 0 + I(x^2) + same(state) #> ) #>  #> # Simulate data #> set.seed(42) #> data = data.frame( #>   x = 1:132, #>   state = rep(c('A', 'B', 'C', 'D'), 33), #>   z = rnorm(132, mean = 1:132, sd = 25), #>   y = 2.  # or whatever signals 'numeric'. Will be replaced by simulation below. #> ) #> empty = mcp(model, data, sample = FALSE, par_x = 'x') #> data$y = empty$simulate(empty, data, #>   cp_1 = 70, #>   cp_2 = 100, #>  #>   Intercept_1 = 10, #>   z_1 = 0.2, #>   x.stateA_1 = -0.30, #>   x.stateB_1 = -0.10, #>   x.stateC_1 = 0.25, #>   x.stateD_1 = 0.50, #>  #>   Intercept_2 = 15, #>   x_2 = -0.8, #>   stateB_2 = 10, #>   stateC_2 = 20, #>   stateD_2 = 30, #>  #>   xE2_3 = 0.02, #>  #>   sigma_1 = 5 #> ) #>  #> # Run sampling #> fit = mcp(model, data, par_x = 'x', sample = sample, seed = 42) #>  #> # Illustrative plot #> if (plot) { #>   set.seed(42) #>   print(plot(fit) + ggplot2::labs(title = 'fit = mcp_example("multiple"); plot(fit)')) #> }  # Without sampling empty = mcp_example("binomial", sample = "none", plot = FALSE) print(empty) #> Family: binomial #> Links: mu = logit #> Segments: #>   1: y | trials(N) ~ 1 #>   2: ~ 0 + x #>   3: ~ 1 + x #>  #> No posterior draws. Nothing to summarise. print(empty$example_code) #> # Define model #> model = list( #>   y | trials(N) ~ 1,  # constant success probability #>   ~ 0 + x,  # joined changing success probability #>   ~ 1 + x  # disjoined changing success probability #> ) #>  #> # Simulate data #> set.seed(42) #> data = data.frame( #>   x = 1:100, #>   N = base::sample(15:25, 100, replace=TRUE), #>   y = 0.  # Numeric placeholder that is valid for every sampled trial count. #> ) #> empty = mcp(model, data, family = binomial(), sample = FALSE) #> data$y = empty$simulate(empty, data, #>   cp_1 = 30, #>   cp_2 = 70, #>   Intercept_1 = 1.5, #>   Intercept_3 = -1, #>   x_2 = -0.15, #>   x_3 = 0.05 #> ) #>  #> # Run sampling #> fit = mcp(model, data, family = binomial(), sample = sample, seed = 42) #>  #> # Illustrative plot #> if (plot) { #>   set.seed(42) #>   print(plot(fit, interval = "fitted") + ggplot2::labs(title = 'fit = mcp_example("binomial"); plot(fit, interval = "fitted")')) #> }  # Now sample this model fit2 = mcp(empty$model, empty$data, family = empty$family, seed = 42) plot(fit2)  # }

Group-level change-point deviations (cp_i_id) follow hierarchical normal distribution around population-level change point truncation. group-specific change points truncated observed range x ordered, population-level change point generally close mean, exactly. Predictor group-level deviations (Intercept_1_id) use standard hierarchical zero-mean priors, without bounds.
